implementation_notes: asyncio runs one thread, so the check-and-insert into a dict is atomic as long as no await separates them; the idiom is a dict from key to the in-flight Task (or a Future created with loop.create_future()) plus, when the section before the insert can await, an asyncio.Lock around it. Task is the shareable completion handle: many coroutines may await the same task and its result or exception is memoised for all of them; a done callback or a finally in the wrapper removes the key so only in-flight work is retained. The language still does not provide the registry itself, which is why this is an idiom rather than a library primitive.
code_sketch:
_inflight = {}                                  # key -> asyncio.Task

async def load(key: str, fetch):
    task = _inflight.get(key)
    if task is not None:
        return await task                       # join the flight
    task = asyncio.create_task(fetch(key))      # created before any await
    _inflight.setdefault(key, task)             # single-threaded: no await here
    try:
        return await task
    finally:
        if _inflight.get(key) is task:
            del _inflight[key]                  # forget on completion
pitfalls: Create the task synchronously: if any await sits between the lookup and the insert, two coroutines can both miss and both start the work.
Delete the entry when the task completes, and delete conditionally (only if the stored task is still the same object) so a late completion cannot evict a newer flight.
An exception retrieved by nobody raises 'Task exception was never retrieved'; retrieving the exception is part of the contract, and every waiter sees the same one.
Cancelling a waiter's await does not cancel the shared task - but wrapping the shared task in a per-caller asyncio.wait_for cancels it for everyone; give waiters a race instead.
The registry is per event loop: work handed to threads or another loop needs its own registry, otherwise entries mix across loops.

variants.name: concurrent.futures map under a threading.Lock
variants.implementation_notes: In threaded code the same registry holds concurrent.futures.Future objects: the first caller registers a future under the lock and submits the work to a ThreadPoolExecutor, later callers take the future out and call result(), which blocks until completion and returns the value or re-raises the stored exception for each of them. set_result/set_exception is what replaces the classic broadcast - any number of threads may block in result(). Hold the lock only for the registry access, never across the computation, or coalescing degrades into global serialization.
variants.code_sketch:
_lock = threading.Lock(); _inflight = {}; _pool = ThreadPoolExecutor()

def load(key, fetch):
    with _lock:
        fut = _inflight.get(key)
        if fut is None:
            fut = _pool.submit(fetch, key)              # the leader runs once
            _inflight[key] = fut                        # register before publishing
            fut.add_done_callback(lambda f, k=key: _forget(k, f))
    return fut.result()                                 # shared value or error

def _forget(key, fut):
    with _lock: _inflight.pop(key, None)                # forget on completion
pitfalls: Hold the registry lock only for map access; computing under the lock makes coalescing indistinguishable from global serialization.
concurrent.futures.Future memoises its result or exception and result() re-raises the same exception object to every waiter; sharing a mutable result corrupts the shared answer.

Publish through the future's completion contract (submit, or set_result/set_exception when the work runs elsewhere) and remove the entry on completion even on failure, or the key stays in flight forever.
The registry is per process and per interpreter: forked workers and other processes do not share it, so multi-process servers still duplicate per worker.
A future whose waiters have all left keeps the error unobserved; retrieve it explicitly so suppressed failures are still logged.
